transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Yeah, um… I came because it’s getting hard to explain things at work in a way people can follow. I’m a supervisor in retail, so I’m supposed to be clear about inventory numbers and the weekend schedule and all that, and I’ll start trying to say something simple, like about the truck delivery or who’s working Thursday, and then my words sort of jump.

Like I’ll be talking about trucks, then somehow I’m on Thursdays, then the church grill—because that was something I was thinking about, I guess—and then my boss’s tone, the way he said something, and I can tell people are looking at me like they don’t know where I’m going with it. And I’m trying to make a point, I really am, but it comes out all mixed together, and then I get more frustrated because I can see I’ve lost them. That’s mostly why I came in.
Have you also noticed changes like needing much less sleep than usual, feeling unusually energetic or 'speeded up,' or having racing thoughts along with this trouble organizing your speech?

I don’t know that I’d call it that, exactly. I mean, I’m tired a lot, especially after work, because by the end of a shift I feel like I’ve been trying to hold a whole stack of papers in the wind, if that makes sense. But needing much less sleep… I haven’t really noticed that as some big change.

And “speeded up,” I’m not sure. My thoughts do feel like they get tangled, but not like I’m suddenly full of energy or staying up all night feeling great. It’s more like I’m trying to say one thing and then another thought cuts across it, and then I’m trying to back up and explain the first thing, and by then the other person is already confused. So… I’m not sure if that’s racing thoughts the way you mean it. It doesn’t feel good or energized. It feels messy.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds others don't seem to hear, or having thoughts or beliefs that others find strange or hard to accept?

Um… I don’t know. Not in a way I can really point to and say, “Yes, that’s happening.” I mean, sometimes in the store there’s a lot of noise—the scanners, the carts, people talking over the radios—and I might think I heard someone say my name, but then it’s just the regular commotion, or somebody talking to someone else. I don’t think I’m hearing voices, like… like a person talking to me when nobody’s there. At least I don’t think so.

And beliefs, I’m not sure what counts as strange. I know people at work sometimes don’t follow what I’m saying, and then they look at me funny, but that might just be because I’m not explaining it right. I haven’t really had someone tell me, “That belief is impossible,” or anything like that. It’s more that I get tangled up trying to get the thought out, and then it probably sounds odd by the time I’ve said it. But as far as hearing things other people don’t hear, or having some big unusual belief… I don’t have a clear example of that.

Have you noticed any recent changes in your memory or ability to concentrate on tasks—like forgetting things you normally would remember, or losing track of what you were doing—that are new compared to how you used to be?

I’m not sure I can say there’s a new memory problem, exactly. I mean, I’m 59, so I’ll forget where I put my keys sometimes, or I’ll walk into the back room and have to pause for a second like, “What did I come back here for?” But I don’t know if that’s new or just normal life, work being busy, too many things happening at once.

Concentration… that’s harder to answer. At work I do lose the thread sometimes, but it feels more like when I’m trying to explain something or keep several details in my head at the same time, it all gets crowded. Like I’ll be checking a delivery list, then someone asks me about a schedule change, and then I have to remember what number I was on, and I might need to go back and look again. But I don’t know if my concentration itself has changed, or if I’m just getting thrown off because there’s so much going on.

I wouldn’t say I’m forgetting major things I normally wouldn’t remember. It’s more… I notice I have to double-check myself more, but I can’t tell if that’s because my memory is worse or because I’m second-guessing myself after people don’t follow what I’m saying. So, I guess the honest answer is I haven’t noticed a clear, new memory change. It’s more just feeling disorganized when I’m trying to keep track of things.
How long has this problem with your words and thoughts getting jumbled while speaking been going on—days, weeks, or months?

I’d say… months, not days or weeks. It’s hard to put an exact date on it because it kind of crept up, and at first I thought I was just tired or having an off day. But the jumbled explanations, and those odd pauses where I’m standing there on the sales floor trying to get the sentence back in order—that’s been noticeable for about six months now.

I remember because it’s been long enough that it’s not just one bad week. It’s like I started realizing, “Okay, this is happening again,” when I’d be trying to explain something to someone at work and I could feel the words getting turned around before they came out. So… around six months, I think.

When this happens, do you find yourself struggling to come up with the specific word or name for something—even though you know exactly what you mean—or is it more that your ideas themselves seem to jump from one topic to another?

It’s more the second one, I think. Not so much that I can’t find the word, like the word for “stapler” or somebody’s name is sitting there and I can’t grab it. That happens sometimes, sure, but that’s not really what I came in about.

It’s more like the ideas start… jumping tracks. Like I’ll be trying to explain the inventory numbers to someone, or go over the weekend schedule, and I know there’s a point I’m trying to make. But then I’ll go from the truck delivery, to Thursday, to whether the church grill thing is changing who can work Saturday, and then somehow I’m talking about my boss’s tone when he asked about it, and by then people are just looking at me like they can’t follow where I’m going.

And I can feel it happening while I’m talking, which makes it worse, because then I try to pull it back and explain the connection, but the connection takes another detour. So it’s not exactly missing a word. It’s like the words are there, but the path between the thoughts doesn’t stay straight.
Have you had any recent head injuries, seizures, strokes, or other neurological symptoms—like weakness, numbness, vision changes, or headaches—around the time this started?

I don’t think so. I mean, nothing that I can connect to when this started. I didn’t hit my head or have some big accident or anything like that, at least not that I remember. No episode where I blacked out and then the talking got strange afterward.

As far as seizures or a stroke, I wouldn’t know exactly what all that feels like, but I haven’t had anything where one side stopped working or I couldn’t see right all of a sudden, or some dramatic thing like that. If you mean headaches, I get normal ones now and then like anyone, especially when work is stressful, but I can’t say there was some new headache problem that came along with this.

It really didn’t feel like there was a clear “event,” if that’s what you’re asking. It was more like I slowly started noticing people weren’t following me, and then I started noticing myself getting tangled up while talking. So… no, not that I’m aware of.

Do you have any ongoing medical conditions—like diabetes, thyroid problems, liver or kidney issues—or do you drink alcohol or use any substances regularly, and if so, did anything change with those around the time this speech and thought problem started six months ago?

I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I mean, as far as I know, I don’t have anything like that going on—at least nothing someone has sat me down and said, “You have diabetes,” or “You have thyroid trouble,” or liver or kidney problems. I’m not saying I’ve been perfect about getting every checkup exactly on time, but there hasn’t been some medical thing that started right when this talking problem started.

Alcohol or substances… I don’t really have anything I can point to there either. Nothing changed around six months ago that makes me think, “Oh, that’s when I started doing this,” and then my thoughts got mixed up. I guess that’s part of what bothers me, honestly, because if there were a clear cause like that, it would make more sense to me.

So, no—nothing I’m aware of with medical conditions or drinking or substances changing around that time. At least not that I’ve noticed.

Aside from the trouble organizing your speech, have you noticed any new difficulty handling everyday tasks—like paying bills, managing your medications, or using appliances you've always known how to use?

Yeah… I mean, not exactly like I forgot how to use the microwave or something. It’s not that kind of thing, at least not in the way you’re saying it. But everyday responsibilities have gotten harder because people don’t seem to trust me with them the same way now.

At work, that’s where it’s been the most obvious. I used to run the busy weekend shifts a lot, and now I’m not really trusted to do that anymore. They’ll say it’s just “coverage” or “balancing the schedule,” but I can tell. And after my performance review, my boss was pretty direct that if things don’t improve, I could be suspended. That was… that was hard to hear, because I’ve done this kind of work for a long time, and I have a degree, and I’m used to being the person other people come to when things are messy.

At home it’s been embarrassing too. My wife has had to step in and cover commitments I used to handle, because people started getting uncomfortable or confused around me. Like I’ll be trying to coordinate something or talk through a plan, and then afterward she’ll sort of smooth it over or just take it on herself. I don’t think it’s that I can’t do basic things, but the way I come across makes the tasks fall apart, if that makes sense.

Over these past six months, have you noticed yourself feeling less interested in socializing with friends or family, showing less emotion than you used to, or losing motivation to do things you normally enjoy?

I’m not sure. I mean, I understand what you’re asking, but I don’t know if I can separate that from everything else that’s been going on.

Like with socializing, I wouldn’t say I suddenly stopped caring about people. I still care about my wife, my family, people I know. But I guess I haven’t been as eager to put myself in situations where I have to explain myself a lot, because it gets tiring when people look at you like they’re waiting for you to land the plane, you know? So if I’m quieter or I don’t push to go out as much, I don’t know if that’s “less interest” exactly or just not wanting another awkward conversation.

As far as emotion… I don’t think I feel blank inside. I get upset, embarrassed, frustrated. Maybe I don’t show it the same way because I’m trying to keep myself together, especially when I can tell someone is confused by me. But I don’t know that I’d say I’ve lost emotion.

Motivation is kind of the same. I still want things to go well. I still want to do the things I normally do. It’s just harder when I’m worried I’m going to mess up explaining something or people are going to misunderstand me. So… I guess I haven’t noticed some big loss of interest or motivation exactly. It’s more complicated than that, at least from my side.

Have you noticed yourself feeling unusually suspicious or wary of other people's intentions lately—like wondering if coworkers or others are talking about you, watching you, or trying to undermine you?

I don’t know that I’d call it suspicious exactly. I mean… I’ve wondered what people are thinking, sure, especially when conversations get strange or when I can tell I didn’t explain something right. At work, if people lower their voices or stop talking when I come by, I notice it more than I used to, but I don’t know if that means they’re talking about me or if I’m just more sensitive because I already feel on edge about how I’m coming across.

I wouldn’t say I feel like people are watching me or plotting against me. It’s more like… I’m aware of the room, maybe too aware. If my coworkers seem careful around me, I start trying to figure out whether I said something odd, or whether they’re worried I’ll mess something up, or whether I’m just reading too much into it. And with my boss, after everything that’s been said, it’s hard not to feel scrutinized, but that also might just be the situation.

So no, not in the sense that I’m convinced people are out to get me. I just feel more guarded, I guess, because I don’t always know how I’m being received.

When you try to write something down—like a note or an email—instead of speaking it, do your thoughts stay organized and easy to follow, or do they still jump around the same way they do when you're talking?

Writing helps a little, but not as much as I wish it did. I used to think maybe if I just put it in an email, it would come out cleaner, because I could slow down and not have people watching me while I’m trying to explain. But even then, it can still kind of… branch off.

Like if I’m trying to write something simple about inventory numbers or the weekend schedule, I’ll start with the actual point, like which delivery truck came in or who’s supposed to work Thursday, and then somehow I’m adding something about the church grill thing from another conversation, or how my boss said something in a certain tone, and then I’m back to the schedule again. In my head it feels connected while I’m writing it, like I’m trying to give the full picture so nobody misunderstands me, but when I read it back—or when someone replies confused—I can see that it jumped around.

That’s actually a big part of why I came in. It isn’t only when I’m talking out loud. The talking is more obvious because people’s faces change right there in front of me, but with writing it still happens. I’ll look at an email and think, “Okay, this was supposed to be about weekend coverage, so why did I mention the truck, Thursday, the grill, and my boss’s tone all in one paragraph?” It’s embarrassing, because I know what I’m trying to say, but it doesn’t always come out in a straight line.

Aside from the trouble organizing your speech, have you or others noticed you acting in ways that seem unusual or out of character—like odd or disorganized behavior, unusual movements, or trouble completing routine actions in the expected order?

Yeah… I think there have been some things like that, though I don’t know how odd they look from the outside until someone points it out.

At work, especially on the sales floor, I’ll sometimes realize I’ve been pacing the same aisle for no real reason. Not walking somewhere to get something, just sort of going back and forth like I’m trying to start a task but not actually starting it. Or I’ll straighten the same row of batteries over and over—like I’ll line them up, step away, come back, fix them again, even though they’re already fine. In the moment it feels like I’m doing something useful, like I’m keeping things in order, but then I notice I haven’t moved on to what I was supposed to be doing.

And there have been times where I’m standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand, and the associates are kind of waiting for me to tell them where to go or what needs covering, and I just… stall out. I know I’m supposed to give directions, and I know what the clipboard is for, but it’s like I’m holding the thing and not getting to the next step. Then I feel everyone looking at me, and that makes it worse because I’m trying to hurry up and act normal, but I’m still stuck there for a minute.

So yes, I guess that would count as unusual for me. I used to be pretty automatic with that stuff—walk the floor, check the endcaps, assign breaks, handle the schedule. Lately sometimes I get caught in these little loops or pauses, and it’s embarrassing because I’m supposed to be the person keeping everyone else moving.

doctor.question: Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds others don't seem to hear, or having thoughts or beliefs that others find strange or hard to accept?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hallucinations or delusional beliefs, but the provided symptom profile only covers disorganized thinking/speech, disorganized behavior, impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
Um… I don’t know. Not in a way I can really point to and say, “Yes, that’s happening.” I mean, sometimes in the store there’s a lot of noise—the scanners, the carts, people talking over the radios—and I might think I heard someone say my name, but then it’s just the regular commotion, or somebody talking to someone else. I don’t think I’m hearing voices, like… like a person talking to me when nobody’s there. At least I don’t think so.

And beliefs, I’m not sure what counts as strange. I know people at work sometimes don’t follow what I’m saying, and then they look at me funny, but that might just be because I’m not explaining it right. I haven’t really had someone tell me, “That belief is impossible,” or anything like that. It’s more that I get tangled up trying to get the thought out, and then it probably sounds odd by the time I’ve said it. But as far as hearing things other people don’t hear, or having some big unusual belief… I don’t have a clear example of that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the speech disorganization is part of a broader pattern of memory or cognitive decline (suggesting an organic cognitive disorder) versus a lifelong attentional pattern, by asking about recent changes in memory or concentration.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any recent changes in your memory or ability to concentrate on tasks—like forgetting things you normally would remember, or losing track of what you were doing—that are new compared to how you used to be?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about memory or concentration changes, such as forgetting or losing track of tasks. The provided symptom profiles cover disorganized speech/thinking, abnormal behavior, impairment, and duration, but not memory or concentration symptoms specifically.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I can say there’s a new memory problem, exactly. I mean, I’m 59, so I’ll forget where I put my keys sometimes, or I’ll walk into the back room and have to pause for a second like, “What did I come back here for?” But I don’t know if that’s new or just normal life, work being busy, too many things happening at once.

Concentration… that’s harder to answer. At work I do lose the thread sometimes, but it feels more like when I’m trying to explain something or keep several details in my head at the same time, it all gets crowded. Like I’ll be checking a delivery list, then someone asks me about a schedule change, and then I have to remember what number I was on, and I might need to go back and look again. But I don’t know if my concentration itself has changed, or if I’m just getting thrown off because there’s so much going on.

I wouldn’t say I’m forgetting major things I normally wouldn’t remember. It’s more… I notice I have to double-check myself more, but I can’t tell if that’s because my memory is worse or because I’m second-guessing myself after people don’t follow what I’m saying. So, I guess the honest answer is I haven’t noticed a clear, new memory change. It’s more just feeling disorganized when I’m trying to keep track of things.

inference.note: No manic/hypomanic symptoms reported (denies decreased sleep need, elevated energy, racing thoughts), lowering likelihood of F90.0 given onset at age 59 with no childhood history noted; retained F20.9 given disorganized speech/derailment, F06.7 given age and possible mild cognitive contribution, and F41.1 given frustration/anxiety about symptoms. No clear hallucinations or fixed delusions reported, but speech disorganization remains prominent.

doctor.intent: Determine how long the disorganized speech/thought pattern has been occurring, which is critical for differentiating a psychotic disorder (requiring longer duration) from an anxiety-related or cognitive etiology
doctor.question: How long has this problem with your words and thoughts getting jumbled while speaking been going on—days, weeks, or months?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The jumbled explanations and odd stops on the sales floor have been noticeable for about six months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how long the jumbled words and thoughts while speaking have been going on, which matches the duration of the noticeable psychotic/disorganized speech symptoms.

patient.answer:
I’d say… months, not days or weeks. It’s hard to put an exact date on it because it kind of crept up, and at first I thought I was just tired or having an off day. But the jumbled explanations, and those odd pauses where I’m standing there on the sales floor trying to get the sentence back in order—that’s been noticeable for about six months now.

I remember because it’s been long enough that it’s not just one bad week. It’s like I started realizing, “Okay, this is happening again,” when I’d be trying to explain something to someone at work and I could feel the words getting turned around before they came out. So… around six months, I think.

inference.note: No mania/hypomania features (ruling against pure F41.1 as primary explanation), no clear hallucinations or delusions reported, but symptom is a 6-month insidious progressive disorganized speech/word-finding difficulty in a 59-year-old without mood elevation—raising concern for an early neurocognitive/dementia process (e.g., primary progressive aphasia) or other organic etiology. Removed F41.1 as unsupported by anxiety symptoms; added G30.9 and F09 to consider organic/neurocognitive causes given age and chronic progressive course.

doctor.intent: Assess for aphasia/word-finding difficulty (anomia) versus disorganized thought process, to help distinguish a neurocognitive disorder from a primary psychotic thought disorder
doctor.question: When this happens, do you find yourself struggling to come up with the specific word or name for something—even though you know exactly what you mean—or is it more that your ideas themselves seem to jump from one topic to another?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when I try to explain inventory numbers or the weekend schedule, my words start jumping from trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss’s tone, and people look at me like they can’t follow what I’m saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the speaking problem is word-finding difficulty or thoughts jumping between topics, which directly matches disorganized thinking and speech.

patient.answer:
It’s more the second one, I think. Not so much that I can’t find the word, like the word for “stapler” or somebody’s name is sitting there and I can’t grab it. That happens sometimes, sure, but that’s not really what I came in about.

It’s more like the ideas start… jumping tracks. Like I’ll be trying to explain the inventory numbers to someone, or go over the weekend schedule, and I know there’s a point I’m trying to make. But then I’ll go from the truck delivery, to Thursday, to whether the church grill thing is changing who can work Saturday, and then somehow I’m talking about my boss’s tone when he asked about it, and by then people are just looking at me like they can’t follow where I’m going.

And I can feel it happening while I’m talking, which makes it worse, because then I try to pull it back and explain the connection, but the connection takes another detour. So it’s not exactly missing a word. It’s like the words are there, but the path between the thoughts doesn’t stay straight.

doctor.intent: Assess for an underlying medical/neurological cause (e.g., head injury, stroke, seizures, or other neurological symptoms) that could explain the thought disorganization, to differentiate an organic mental disorder from a primary psychotic illness.
doctor.question: Have you had any recent head injuries, seizures, strokes, or other neurological symptoms—like weakness, numbness, vision changes, or headaches—around the time this started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about possible neurological causes or associated symptoms such as head injury, seizures, stroke, weakness, numbness, vision changes, or headaches, which are not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so. I mean, nothing that I can connect to when this started. I didn’t hit my head or have some big accident or anything like that, at least not that I remember. No episode where I blacked out and then the talking got strange afterward.

As far as seizures or a stroke, I wouldn’t know exactly what all that feels like, but I haven’t had anything where one side stopped working or I couldn’t see right all of a sudden, or some dramatic thing like that. If you mean headaches, I get normal ones now and then like anyone, especially when work is stressful, but I can’t say there was some new headache problem that came along with this.

It really didn’t feel like there was a clear “event,” if that’s what you’re asking. It was more like I slowly started noticing people weren’t following me, and then I started noticing myself getting tangled up while talking. So… no, not that I’m aware of.

inference.note: No manic symptoms, hallucinations, or clear neurological deficits/events reported, but insidious 6-month course of tangential/circumstantial speech (derailment) without anomia, preserved insight into the disorganization, and lack of clear psychotic or mood features keeps mild cognitive/psychotic-spectrum and organic causes open; no narrowing yet.

doctor.intent: Assess for an underlying general medical condition or substance/alcohol use (e.g., diabetes, thyroid disease, liver/kidney problems, heavy alcohol use) that began or worsened around the same time as the speech/thought difficulties, to help distinguish an organic cause from a primary psychiatric disorder.
doctor.question: Do you have any ongoing medical conditions—like diabetes, thyroid problems, liver or kidney issues—or do you drink alcohol or use any substances regularly, and if so, did anything change with those around the time this speech and thought problem started six months ago?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about medical conditions or substance/alcohol use as possible causes or contributors, which is not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not really sure how to answer that in a clean way. I mean, as far as I know, I don’t have anything like that going on—at least nothing someone has sat me down and said, “You have diabetes,” or “You have thyroid trouble,” or liver or kidney problems. I’m not saying I’ve been perfect about getting every checkup exactly on time, but there hasn’t been some medical thing that started right when this talking problem started.

Alcohol or substances… I don’t really have anything I can point to there either. Nothing changed around six months ago that makes me think, “Oh, that’s when I started doing this,” and then my thoughts got mixed up. I guess that’s part of what bothers me, honestly, because if there were a clear cause like that, it would make more sense to me.

So, no—nothing I’m aware of with medical conditions or drinking or substances changing around that time. At least not that I’ve noticed.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is broader cognitive/functional decline (e.g., managing finances, medications, or familiar tasks) beyond the speech disorganization, which would point toward a dementia/cognitive disorder rather than an isolated thought-disorder process like schizophrenia.
doctor.question: Aside from the trouble organizing your speech, have you noticed any new difficulty handling everyday tasks—like paying bills, managing your medications, or using appliances you've always known how to use?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m not trusted to run busy weekend shifts anymore, and after the performance review my boss warned me I could be suspended if things don’t improve. At home, my wife has had to cover commitments I used to handle because people started getting uncomfortable or confused around me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms are causing difficulty managing everyday responsibilities and functioning beyond speech organization.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, not exactly like I forgot how to use the microwave or something. It’s not that kind of thing, at least not in the way you’re saying it. But everyday responsibilities have gotten harder because people don’t seem to trust me with them the same way now.

At work, that’s where it’s been the most obvious. I used to run the busy weekend shifts a lot, and now I’m not really trusted to do that anymore. They’ll say it’s just “coverage” or “balancing the schedule,” but I can tell. And after my performance review, my boss was pretty direct that if things don’t improve, I could be suspended. That was… that was hard to hear, because I’ve done this kind of work for a long time, and I have a degree, and I’m used to being the person other people come to when things are messy.

At home it’s been embarrassing too. My wife has had to step in and cover commitments I used to handle, because people started getting uncomfortable or confused around me. Like I’ll be trying to coordinate something or talk through a plan, and then afterward she’ll sort of smooth it over or just take it on herself. I don’t think it’s that I can’t do basic things, but the way I come across makes the tasks fall apart, if that makes sense.

inference.note: No memory decline, functional loss in ADLs beyond speech, or medical/substance cause identified, reducing likelihood of G30.9 (Alzheimer's) and F09 (mental disorder due to medical condition). Persistent disorganized speech/thought derailment for 6 months without manic or clear psychotic symptoms keeps F20.9 as leading candidate; F06.7 retained pending further cognitive workup.

doctor.intent: Assess for negative symptoms characteristic of schizophrenia (e.g., blunted affect, social withdrawal, diminished motivation) that would be less expected in a mild cognitive disorder
doctor.question: Over these past six months, have you noticed yourself feeling less interested in socializing with friends or family, showing less emotion than you used to, or losing motivation to do things you normally enjoy?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about negative symptoms such as reduced social interest, diminished emotional expression, and loss of motivation, which are not covered by the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure. I mean, I understand what you’re asking, but I don’t know if I can separate that from everything else that’s been going on.

Like with socializing, I wouldn’t say I suddenly stopped caring about people. I still care about my wife, my family, people I know. But I guess I haven’t been as eager to put myself in situations where I have to explain myself a lot, because it gets tiring when people look at you like they’re waiting for you to land the plane, you know? So if I’m quieter or I don’t push to go out as much, I don’t know if that’s “less interest” exactly or just not wanting another awkward conversation.

As far as emotion… I don’t think I feel blank inside. I get upset, embarrassed, frustrated. Maybe I don’t show it the same way because I’m trying to keep myself together, especially when I can tell someone is confused by me. But I don’t know that I’d say I’ve lost emotion.

Motivation is kind of the same. I still want things to go well. I still want to do the things I normally do. It’s just harder when I’m worried I’m going to mess up explaining something or people are going to misunderstand me. So… I guess I haven’t noticed some big loss of interest or motivation exactly. It’s more complicated than that, at least from my side.

inference.note: No new information rules out either candidate. Tangential/derailed speech (formal thought disorder) without mood elevation, hallucinations, memory/executive decline, or clear negative symptoms remains consistent with a primary psychotic process (F20.9) or a mild neurocognitive disorder affecting complex language organization (F06.7). No evidence of substance use, medical illness, or focal neurological findings to explain symptoms otherwise.

doctor.intent: Assess for paranoid or suspicious thinking that would support a primary psychotic process (schizophrenia) rather than a cognitive disorder due to a medical condition
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself feeling unusually suspicious or wary of other people's intentions lately—like wondering if coworkers or others are talking about you, watching you, or trying to undermine you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suspiciousness or paranoid ideas, but the provided symptom profile only covers disorganized thinking/speech, disorganized behavior, functional impairment, and duration.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it suspicious exactly. I mean… I’ve wondered what people are thinking, sure, especially when conversations get strange or when I can tell I didn’t explain something right. At work, if people lower their voices or stop talking when I come by, I notice it more than I used to, but I don’t know if that means they’re talking about me or if I’m just more sensitive because I already feel on edge about how I’m coming across.

I wouldn’t say I feel like people are watching me or plotting against me. It’s more like… I’m aware of the room, maybe too aware. If my coworkers seem careful around me, I start trying to figure out whether I said something odd, or whether they’re worried I’ll mess something up, or whether I’m just reading too much into it. And with my boss, after everything that’s been said, it’s hard not to feel scrutinized, but that also might just be the situation.

So no, not in the sense that I’m convinced people are out to get me. I just feel more guarded, I guess, because I don’t always know how I’m being received.

inference.note: No clear negative symptoms (blunted affect, anhedonia) or fixed paranoid delusions were elicited, and no evidence of substance or medical etiology, so both schizophrenia and organic/cognitive disorder with disorganized thought remain viable; list unchanged.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the thought disorganization is specific to spontaneous speech (suggesting an underlying cognitive/attentional deficit, as in F06.7) or also occurs in other modalities like writing (suggesting a pervasive formal thought disorder, as in F20.9)
doctor.question: When you try to write something down—like a note or an email—instead of speaking it, do your thoughts stay organized and easy to follow, or do they still jump around the same way they do when you're talking?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Thinking_Speech
target_item.manifestation: I came in because when I try to explain inventory numbers or the weekend schedule, my words start jumping from trucks to Thursdays to the church grill to my boss’s tone, and people look at me like they can’t follow what I’m saying.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the patient's thoughts remain disorganized when writing, which directly concerns scattered, hard-to-follow thought and communication.

patient.answer:
Writing helps a little, but not as much as I wish it did. I used to think maybe if I just put it in an email, it would come out cleaner, because I could slow down and not have people watching me while I’m trying to explain. But even then, it can still kind of… branch off.

Like if I’m trying to write something simple about inventory numbers or the weekend schedule, I’ll start with the actual point, like which delivery truck came in or who’s supposed to work Thursday, and then somehow I’m adding something about the church grill thing from another conversation, or how my boss said something in a certain tone, and then I’m back to the schedule again. In my head it feels connected while I’m writing it, like I’m trying to give the full picture so nobody misunderstands me, but when I read it back—or when someone replies confused—I can see that it jumped around.

That’s actually a big part of why I came in. It isn’t only when I’m talking out loud. The talking is more obvious because people’s faces change right there in front of me, but with writing it still happens. I’ll look at an email and think, “Okay, this was supposed to be about weekend coverage, so why did I mention the truck, Thursday, the grill, and my boss’s tone all in one paragraph?” It’s embarrassing, because I know what I’m trying to say, but it doesn’t always come out in a straight line.

inference.note: Writing sample confirms disorganized thought process (tangentiality/derailment) present in both spoken and written language, occurring without mood elevation, hallucinations, fixed delusions, or clear cognitive/memory decline, and without medical/substance cause. This supports a primary thought disorder (schizophrenia spectrum, F20.9) or a mild neurocognitive-like disorganization (F06.7) still under consideration; no new findings ruled out either candidate.

doctor.intent: Assess for grossly disorganized or unusual behavior (a core schizophrenia symptom) beyond speech, to help differentiate a primary psychotic disorder from a cognitive disorder due to a general medical condition
doctor.question: Aside from the trouble organizing your speech, have you or others noticed you acting in ways that seem unusual or out of character—like odd or disorganized behavior, unusual movements, or trouble completing routine actions in the expected order?

target_item.name: Disorganized_Abnormal_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes on the sales floor I catch myself pacing the same aisle, straightening the same row of batteries over and over, or just standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand while the associates are waiting for me to tell them what to do.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about unusual or disorganized behavior, unusual movements, and trouble completing routine actions, which matches this symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think there have been some things like that, though I don’t know how odd they look from the outside until someone points it out.

At work, especially on the sales floor, I’ll sometimes realize I’ve been pacing the same aisle for no real reason. Not walking somewhere to get something, just sort of going back and forth like I’m trying to start a task but not actually starting it. Or I’ll straighten the same row of batteries over and over—like I’ll line them up, step away, come back, fix them again, even though they’re already fine. In the moment it feels like I’m doing something useful, like I’m keeping things in order, but then I notice I haven’t moved on to what I was supposed to be doing.

And there have been times where I’m standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand, and the associates are kind of waiting for me to tell them where to go or what needs covering, and I just… stall out. I know I’m supposed to give directions, and I know what the clipboard is for, but it’s like I’m holding the thing and not getting to the next step. Then I feel everyone looking at me, and that makes it worse because I’m trying to hurry up and act normal, but I’m still stuck there for a minute.

So yes, I guess that would count as unusual for me. I used to be pretty automatic with that stuff—walk the floor, check the endcaps, assign breaks, handle the schedule. Lately sometimes I get caught in these little loops or pauses, and it’s embarrassing because I’m supposed to be the person keeping everyone else moving.

inference.note: The new findings of stereotyped, purposeless repetitive behaviors (straightening the same items repeatedly) and psychomotor stalling/blocking while holding the clipboard, combined with longstanding disorganized speech/thought (derailment persisting even in writing), functional decline, and lack of any cognitive, medical, or substance-related etiology, support a primary psychotic disorder with disorganized and catatonic-like features rather than a mild neurocognitive disorder. This effectively rules out F06.7.

opening_question.question: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. Can you start by telling me what's been bringing you in to see me?
